We all know that Ubuntu does not remove older kernels. Using an LTS release with a small root partition will fill up that partition pretty quickly. There are packages that will clean this up for you, but when I went to install it, the dependency list was rather large. For something that is essentially a bash script. So I wrote it. You can specify how many kernels you want to keep in the BACK variable.

#!/bin/bash

#Config
BACK=3

#Defines
COUNT=$(dpkg --get-selections linux-image-3* | \
 awk '{print $a}' | wc -l)
LIST=$(dpkg --get-selections linux-image-3* | \
 awk '{print $1}' | \
 cut -d "-" -f 3,4 | \
 head -n `expr $COUNT - $BACK`)

for a in $LIST; do sudo apt-get purge linux-image-$a linux-header-$a; done

After installing a new kernel, reboot and try this:

 dpkg -l 'linux-*' | sed '/^ii/!d;/'"$(uname -r | sed "s/\(.*\)-\([^0-9]\+\)/\1/")"'/d;s/^[^ ]* [^ ]* \([^ ]*\).*/\1/;/[0-9]/!d' | xargs sudo apt-get -y purge

I find that apt can do this for me. After sudo apt-get dist-upgrade installs a new kernel package for me the old one becomes an unneeded auto‐installed dependency and it recommends you run sudo apt-get autoremove to remove it.

Here is the message I get every time I run an update or install a package.

The following packages were automatically installed and are no longer required:
 linux-image-3.19.0-41-generic linux-image-3.19.0-42-generic
 linux-image-3.19.0-43-generic linux-image-3.19.0-47-generic
 linux-image-extra-3.19.0-41-generic linux-image-extra-3.19.0-42-generic
 linux-image-extra-3.19.0-43-generic linux-image-extra-3.19.0-47-generic
Use 'apt-get autoremove' to remove them.

The only thing I have to watch out for is that I have rebooted since installing the newest kernel package to ensure I'm not still running one of the ones that I'm about to remove.

sudo apt-get autoremove --purge really is the best way to clean unneeded packages. If you really feel the need to keep a few old kernels then you can just sudo apt-get purge the oldest ones.
